head: 0320a0d22641e7eccc41254129d31ad957c07f04
summary:
The core mechanism is sound, and the sources back it. CancelSynchronousIo on an OpenThread(THREAD_TERMINATE) handle, a retry after ERROR_NOT_FOUND, a canceller kept off the UI thread, and discarding a call's result by recorded intent all match the Microsoft docs, the Microsoft Q&A report of CancelSynchronousIo blocking behind Defender, and .NET's own PR 72503/87103, which uses this pattern for non-overlapped pipes and files. None of the findings is a blocker, but five need fixing before build.

1. The bracketing invariant depends on each call site remembering it. Every Win32 filesystem call on the scan thread needs the Enter/Exit/Settle bracket, and the design writes it by hand at each site. It also turns down an architecture rule, on the claim that no regex can express it. A regex can, once the bracket lives in a single wrapper file. The build's "list the P/Invokes in Kernel32.cs" step also misses BCL System.IO calls.
2. The existing tests don't run the production path. A guard exists only when ct.CanBeCanceled, and the 86 tests pass CancellationToken.None, so none of them runs the guarded path the app actually uses.
3. An aborted SizeProbe can commit a wrong on-disk size. Nothing says it aborts its containing folder, so an entry with no on-disk size and no ProbeFailed flag could be committed. That breaks a counting rule.
4. The most common real case is the one nobody measured. A share that drops mid-scan is spike 3's stalled session, which never ran. The close after an abort stays unguarded, even though moving it off the scan thread is cheap now.
5. The cloud half rests on a stand-in call. The design marks this question as forcing resynthesis but assigns nobody to settle it. Spike 2 tested FindFirstFileExW, while the scanner really calls GetFileInformationByHandleEx, and the survey identified that. This goes back to risk-spike.

The minor findings cover:
- a successful handle that is discarded but never closed
- the canceller thread's IsBackground setting
- a single-thread check that only runs in Debug builds
- a share test that cannot prove the interrupt caused the return
- a stress test with no way to observe a stray cancel
- the default suite starting SMB (and so NTLM) connections to a random address
- criterion (1) promising what the Microsoft docs say cannot be guaranteed

findings.claim: The design's core invariant is that every Win32 filesystem call on the scan thread goes through Enter/Settle. It holds only as long as each call site remembers it. The bracket (`if(!g.Enter()) return 995; try { e = Call(); } finally { issued = g.Exit(); } return Settle(e, issued)`) is written out by hand at every site: Open, each List buffer call, each SizeProbe call, the root attribute probe and the volume query. Any later call site can leave it out. It can also leave out just Settle, or read the buffer before Settle, which is the spike-2 SUCCESS+empty defect coming back. The design turns down a rule because 'no regex fires on the defect without also firing on correct code', but that is only true while the bracket is copied inline. The way the build finds sites ('listing every P/Invoke in Kernel32.cs') has a second hole: BCL filesystem calls on the scan thread (File/Directory/DirectoryInfo/Path.GetFullPath/DriveInfo on a UNC root) are not in Kernel32.cs. They would block without a guard, and nothing would flag them.
findings.evidence: coherence_check item 6: 'The guard's Enter/Exit bracketing has no regex form ... so it is enforced by the case matrix and the build's enumeration of Kernel32 P/Invokes, not by a rule.' Component 'Scanner: own the guard': 'the build enumerates them by listing every P/Invoke in Kernel32.cs'.
findings.fix: Move the bracket into one seam. Give SynchronousIoCancel (or a GuardedIo class next to it) one method per call, e.g. `int Open(string path, out SafeFileHandle h)`, `int List(SafeFileHandle h, Span<byte> buf, bool restart)` and `int Probe(...)`. Each method does Enter/Call/Exit/Settle itself and disposes anything the call produced when Settle says aborted. Then add an architecture_rule: `\bKernel32\.(CreateFileW|GetFileInformationByHandleEx|<every other fs P/Invoke>)\s*\(` must not match in src/**/*.cs, except in Kernel32.cs and the wrapper file. Add a second rule forbidding `\b(File|Directory|DirectoryInfo|FileInfo|DriveInfo)\.` in src/FsAnalyser.Core/Scanning/**/*.cs, so a new BCL call on the scan thread fails the build instead of blocking without a guard.

findings.claim: The design treats the existing 86 tests as the regression guard for 'a live, never-cancelled token'. But it also says most test scans pass CancellationToken.None, and a None token creates no guard at all. So every counting-rule test, including the unreadable-folder (error 5) test, runs a path the app never uses. MainWindow always passes a live CTS token, so in the app every call goes through Enter/Exit/Settle. That path is exercised only by the new cancel tests, and none of those scans the counting-rule trees. Take a bug where Settle or Exit reports issued=true without a cancel, or the Open wrapper mishandles a handle. Every counting-rule test would still pass, while the shipped app reports every folder as 995. The null-guard branch also adds a second code path to each call site.
findings.evidence: key_decisions: 'A token that cannot be cancelled gets no thread handle, no registration and no canceller ... Most test scans pass CancellationToken.None ... the 86 existing tests and counting-rule tests run the old path unchanged.' cases: 'Scan with a live, never-cancelled token, or CancellationToken.None ... The existing 86 tests are the regression guard.' SynchronousIoCancel: 'created ... only when ct.CanBeCanceled'.
findings.fix: Always create the guard and always bracket. When !ct.CanBeCanceled, skip only OpenThread and the registration. Then every existing test runs the production bracket, and the null-guard branch goes away. Also run the unreadable-folder (error 5) test and at least one other counting-rule tree test with `new CancellationTokenSource().Token` that is never cancelled, and assert the results match the None run.

findings.claim: The design never says what an aborted SizeProbe does to the folder that contains it. Criterion (3) and the whole-folder discard cover an aborted List only. For SizeProbe it says the probe 'writes no size it did not read and no ProbeFailed flag' and that 'Scanner stops at an aborted probe as it does at an aborted listing'. If probes run while a folder's entries are being built or committed, and FolderDone commits the folder after one probe aborts, that folder gets a file with no on-disk size read and no ProbeFailed flag to mark it. The folder's on-disk subtotal is then silently wrong. The project names on-disk size as a counting rule where no corners may be cut, and a cancelled scan's 'partial' state means folders were not reached, not that the committed folders are wrong.
findings.evidence: Component 'SizeProbe: guarded probe': 'It writes no size it did not read and no ProbeFailed flag.' Contract 'Scanner cancel semantics': 'nothing committed for the aborted folder' is stated for listing. Acceptance criterion (3): 'An aborted folder commits nothing.' Survey: SizeProbe.Probe (SizeProbe.cs:62-66) sets ProbeFailed.
findings.fix: State the rule: an aborted probe aborts its containing folder, which commits nothing, exactly as an aborted List does. Add SizeProbe to the second decidable disagreement ('how List/Probe hand entries to FolderDone'), so build checks where the probe runs relative to the commit before writing the discard. Add a case where a probe is aborted mid-folder and the folder ends in the never-reached state.

findings.claim: The imported precondition 'cleanup after an interrupted call returns promptly' is unproven. It covers the most common real instance of this slice's problem: a share that was reachable and then drops mid-scan because of Wi-Fi loss, VPN disconnect or resume from sleep. That is spike 3's stalled, established session, which never ran. Spike 1 covered only the connect phase, where CreateFileW never returned a handle, so it measured no close at all. If the directory handle's CloseHandle waits on an SMB2 CLOSE to a server that doesn't answer, the scan thread blocks in the unguarded close after the abort. Cancel then only moves the hang into cleanup, and criterion (1) fails for that shape. Spike 3's part (a) is also unmeasured: whether CancelSynchronousIo completes an in-flight QUERY_DIRECTORY on a stalled session within 2 s. The design says the off-thread close is 'a small later addition', but it is just as small now, and building it makes the precondition irrelevant.
findings.evidence: key_decisions: 'The close of a handle after an abort is outside the guard and its latency on a stalled session is not designed around ... If measured to block, the fix is an off-thread close, a small later addition.' Imported precondition: 'The cleanup after an interrupted call (CloseHandle, dispose) returns promptly'. Spike 3: NOT RUN (Defender blocks impacket).
findings.fix: Close aborted handles off the scan thread now. When the guard reports aborted, hand the SafeFileHandle to a background closer (an IsBackground thread or a ThreadPool item) and don't dispose it inline. That is about 10 lines and makes the precondition moot. Keep spike 3 as the measurement of part (a). One way to unblock it without impacket: Windows 11 supports SMB on alternative ports (New-SmbMapping exposes -TcpPort, and the spike notes this). Samba on port 4450 under WSL, if WSL is present, frozen with SIGSTOP, gives a stalled established session without a Defender exclusion. A person still has to approve the change of target, which the spike's method forbids.

findings.claim: The design marks a decidable disagreement 'would_force_resynthesis: true' and passes anyway, with nobody assigned to settle it. The cloud half of the slice ('Harden Cancel against blocked ... cloud calls') depends on CancelSynchronousIo freeing the scanner's real listing call. Spike 2 measured only a stand-in. The spike could not identify the real call, but the survey had already recorded it: GetFileInformationByHandleEx with FileIdExtdDirectoryRestartInfo at DirectoryReader.cs:101. The spike's harness still exists: a provider in a separate process and sync-root flag 2, and it ran unelevated with hr=0 for CfRegisterSyncRoot, CfConnectSyncRoot and CfCreatePlaceholders. Re-running it with the real call is cheap. If the answer is no, the design itself says it needs a different mechanism (abandon the thread, or a scanner process), and that should be known before build writes the guard, not after. The design's 'owed as a measurement' names no owner, and build is not set up to stand up a cloud sync-root provider.
findings.evidence: decidable_disagreements[0]: 'Does CancelSynchronousIo interrupt the scanner's actual listing call, GetFileInformationByHandleEx ... would_force_resynthesis: true'. Spike 2 evidence: 'I could not identify the Core scanner's real enumeration call, so these are stand-ins.' Survey criterion 1 evidence: 'the listing loop (GetFileInformationByHandleEx, DirectoryReader.cs:101)'.
findings.fix: Raise an obligation on risk-spike: re-run cloud-fetch-placeholders-cancel with the scanner's own calls (CreateFileW with FILE_LIST_DIRECTORY and BACKUP_SEMANTICS, then GetFileInformationByHandleEx with FileIdExtdDirectoryRestartInfo), the same separate-process provider, and the repeated-cancel loop. Record whether the call returns within 2 s and what it returns. Design is accepted only on a go.

findings.claim: Settle turns any call made under an issued cancel into 995 'whatever the OS returned'. That includes a CreateFileW that succeeded and returned a valid handle. The design says the result is 'discarded' but never says the handle is closed. Discarding a SafeFileHandle without disposing it leaks it until the finalizer runs, and on SMB it keeps a server-side open alive.
findings.evidence: Contract 'DirectoryReader.Open / List ... return 995 for an aborted call': 'The result is 995 whatever the OS returned ... Nothing from that call is delivered.' Tests: 'Settle(0,true)=995'.
findings.fix: State that an aborted Open disposes any handle it got back, through the same off-thread closer as M4. Put this inside the guarded Open wrapper from M1, so call sites cannot forget it.

findings.claim: The canceller is described as 'a background thread named scan-cancel', but `new Thread(...)` in .NET is a foreground thread by default. The loop retries every 25 ms until the call leaves. Microsoft's docs say 'There is no guarantee that underlying drivers correctly support cancellation', and MS Q&A 258819 reports CancelSynchronousIo blocking behind a Defender on-access scan. So the loop can run for as long as a call that can't be cancelled stays blocked. As a foreground thread, it keeps the process alive after the user closes the window, as an invisible process.
findings.evidence: SynchronousIoCancel key_interactions: 'start a background thread named scan-cancel'. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/canceling-pending-i-o-operations: 'There is no guarantee that underlying drivers correctly support cancellation.'
findings.fix: Specify `IsBackground = true` on the canceller thread.

findings.claim: The single-scan-thread invariant is checked only by a Debug.Assert, so the shipped Release exe never checks it. Suppose a later parallel-listing slice hands one guard to its worker threads. CancelSynchronousIo would target the thread that created the guard instead of the blocked worker. Cancel would silently stop interrupting anything, and it could cancel unrelated I/O on the owning thread. The doc note is the only other carrier, and it has to be read to work.
findings.evidence: SynchronousIoCancel responsibility: 'Debug.Assert in Enter that the caller is the creating thread (single scan thread invariant).' Deferral-note component: 'a later slice that lists in parallel must give each worker its own guard.'
findings.fix: Record Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId in the constructor, and have Enter throw InvalidOperationException in every build when the caller differs. That is one int compare per call.

findings.claim: The share test cannot tell an interrupted call from a network that fails naturally between 0.5 s and 2.5 s. The design names this blind spot and leaves it open. It doesn't need to: CancelSynchronousIo returns TRUE only when it found a pending request to cancel. If the guard counted 'cancels that found a request', the test could assert that the interrupt actually landed. The stress test has a related gap. Its assertion 'no stray cancel after Dispose' has nothing observable behind it, so as written it can only check for no exception and no hang.
findings.evidence: Tests: 'Known limit: a network that fails naturally between 0.5 s and 2.5 s could pass the share test without the interrupt being the cause'. Test (6): 'no stray cancel after Dispose'. MS docs: 'If this function cannot find a request to cancel, the return value is 0 (zero), and GetLastError returns ERROR_NOT_FOUND.'
findings.fix: Add an internal counter on the guard for CancelSynchronousIo calls that returned TRUE. Assert it is at least 1 in the share test and in the pipe tests. In the stress test, after each Scan returns, do a short synchronous pipe WaitForConnection on the same thread with a client that connects after about 50 ms, and assert it is not aborted.

findings.claim: The default suite's share test opens an SMB connection to a varying 192.0.2.N on every run. TEST-NET-1 is not routed on the internet, and spike 1 measured a timeout on this network. But a UNC path with an IP address authenticates with NTLM, not Kerberos. On a hostile local network, where someone controls the gateway, a host answering on 445 would receive the developer's NTLMv2 response automatically each time the suite runs. The design also accepts that the same test goes red whenever the network fails fast.
findings.evidence: Tests: 'CancelReturnsFromAScanBlockedOnAnUnreachableShare scans \\192.0.2.N\s (TEST-NET-1, last octet varied per run)'; key_decisions: 'a scan of a TEST-NET-1 share ... in the default suite'.
findings.fix: Record this as an accepted risk next to the offline-red taste choice. Alternatively, measure a local blocker that never sends credentials: a 127.0.0.1 TcpListener that accepts and never answers the SMB NEGOTIATE, reached through an SMB alternative-port mapping (supported on Windows 11). Authentication would never be attempted, and the result would not depend on the network. It needs a measurement before anyone relies on it.

findings.claim: Acceptance criterion (1) is universal: 'A scan blocked in a synchronous Win32 call on the scan thread returns within 2 s of Cancel.' The Microsoft docs say 'other operations can continue toward completion before they are actually canceled' and that driver support is not guaranteed. MS Q&A 258819 shows CancelSynchronousIo blocking on a CreateFile held by Defender over a slow WAN link. Validate can prove the criterion only for the measured shapes: SMB connect and the local pipe. As worded it would either be reported met for shapes nobody measured, or never be satisfiable.
findings.evidence: selection_rationale 'ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA THIS DESIGN OWNS (1)'. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/cancelsynchronousio-func: 'Most types of operations can be canceled immediately; other operations can continue toward completion before they are actually canceled'. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/258819/should-cancelsynchronousio-be-blocking: 'CancelSynchronousIo is also blocking while it waits for the antivirus scan to complete.'
findings.fix: Scope criterion (1) to the shapes that were measured: an unreachable-SMB connect, a local synchronous pipe, and the cloud listing once M5's re-spike is a go. Say that Cancel() on the UI thread returns promptly in all cases. Name stalled sessions and I/O held by a filter driver as unguaranteed.

dimensions_checked.result: Citations checked. [2] ERROR_NOT_FOUND and the THREAD_TERMINATE requirement are supported by learn.microsoft.com/.../cancelsynchronousio-func. [4] 'CancelSynchronousIo can itself block' is supported by MS Q&A 258819: a user's report against Defender on Server 2019, which the MS answerer did not confirm as by design, but that is enough to justify keeping the canceller off the UI thread. The pipe-test mechanism is backed by dotnet/runtime PR 72503, which uses CancelSynchronousIo to cancel non-overlapped WaitForConnection, and PR 87103 extends the same helper to FileStream. That is BCL prior art for the Enter/Exit/retry protocol, and the design did not consult it; the builder can compare. Unfounded: the close-after-abort precondition (M4), and the cloud case resting on a stand-in call (M5).

Walked the Enter/Exit/canceller orderings the design lists. The token-cancel-before-Register case (the callback runs synchronously on the scan thread and the canceller sees Idle) is fine. Found: a successful Open under a cancel leaks its handle (m1). There is also a tiny window where a canceller that has just CASed InCall to CancelIssued fires into the scan thread's unguarded unwind I/O (CloseHandle) before Dispose joins. That is benign because cleanup IRPs are not cancellable, but it means 'a stray cancel can only land on a call already being abandoned' overstates things (partly covered by m4's stress-test observable).
Canceller thread foreground by default (m2). Single-thread invariant checked only in Debug (m3). Off-thread close deferred when it is cheap now (M4).

none: the per-call bracket costs a few Interlocked operations per syscall. One canceller thread per cancel, the 25 ms fixed retry, and ClassifyReadError as a pure function are each the smallest thing that answers a measured failure (spike 2's single cancel never returning, and SUCCESS+empty). The decision not to build a RECALL_ON_DATA_ACCESS check is correctly argued away by discard-by-intent.

An aborted SizeProbe's containing folder is not covered by the whole-folder discard (M3). Criterion (1) is worded universally, against the Microsoft docs (m6). Leaving the Scan/ScanOptions/UI contracts unchanged is consistent with the survey's evidence.

OpenThread failure falls back to boundary cancel, which is fine. The canceller ignores ERROR_NOT_FOUND. It does not distinguish other CancelSynchronousIo failures (e.g. ACCESS_DENIED or INVALID_HANDLE), so it would loop silently at 40 Hz until the call returns. That is not a hang, and m4's counter would expose it. The unguarded close after an abort is the real open error path (M4).

The design narrows the build check's derived criterion 2 so that 995 without a cancel stays Unreadable. That is consistent with the counting rules and correctly argued. Overriding 'cannot be tested unelevated' rests on spike 1's measurement, which is legitimate. Drift: a disagreement marked would-force-resynthesis is carried past design with no owner (M5, obligation on risk-spike).

The two declared architecture rules are correct. `\bGetCurrentThread\b` does not match GetCurrentThreadId, and CancelSynchronousIo is confined to two files. The missing rule is the one that matters: raw filesystem P/Invokes and BCL IO bypassing the guard (M1).

The counting-rule tests run without a guard, while the app always runs with one (M2). The share test cannot prove causation, and the stress test's stray-cancel assertion has nothing observable (m4). The cloud case has no suite test by design, which is acceptable only after M5's re-spike. The case matrix is otherwise thorough (pre-kernel cancel, refusal after cancel, Settle and Classify tables).

OpenThread(THREAD_TERMINATE) on the process's own thread is harmless and never exposed. The default-suite SMB attempt to an arbitrary IP can leak NTLM on a hostile LAN (m5). No admin operation is needed, and none of the listed ones (whoami, read-denied-folders) would help spike 3, which needs a Defender exclusion or a different SMB server, both of which a person has to decide.
